planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ogon spiraea holds its bright gold foliage color best in full sun and greens up somewhat in shade.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ogon spiraea holds its bright gold foliage color best in full sun and greens up somewhat in shade. Fine, narrow, willow-like leaves emerge bright golden-yellow in spring and hold good color through summer before turning shades of orange and copper in fall, providing season-long foliage interest on a graceful, arching shrub that is also covered in small white flowers along bare branches in very early spring, ahead of the emerging gold foliage. Its combination of early spring bloom and vivid, long-lasting golden foliage makes it a valuable multi-season color accent for a mixed shrub border, standing out clearly against green-leaved companions from spring through fall. Prune lightly after flowering to shape, and provide full sun for the brightest, most sustained gold foliage color through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; birchleaf spirea is a tough, adaptable native tolerant of a range of soil conditions.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; birchleaf spirea is a tough, adaptable native tolerant of a range of soil conditions. Rounded, toothed leaves resembling those of a birch tree cover a low, mounding native shrub topped with flat clusters of small white flowers in late spring and early summer, followed by reliable orange-red fall foliage color, native to open woods and rocky slopes across northern and western North America. Its compact, tidy, mounding habit and tolerance of a range of soils and light conditions make it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a native shrub border, foundation planting, or mass planting where a smaller-scale flowering shrub is wanted. Prune lightly after flowering to shape if needed, and expect minimal pest or disease problems from this tough, adaptable native species.
